## Fate of 11 state laws in balance

On Dec. 2, the Supreme Court will take up a challenge to Connecticut’s move, soon after the Sandy Hook mass shooting, to outlaw AR-15 and similar platform semiautomatic rifles. That case, Grant v. Higgins, is consolidated with the lead case, Khaya v. Cook County, in which the justices will consider a 1993 ordinance in prohibiting AR-15-style rifles in Cook County, Illinois, which includes Chicago.

In practical terms, the Cook County ordinance has been superseded by an Illinois statute enacted after a mass shooting at the 2022 Fourth of July parade in the Chicago suburb of Highland Park, in which seven people were killed and 50 wounded.

Besides Connecticut and Illinois, 11 other states prohibit AR-15-style weapons, and the fate of those laws are on the table in the consolidated cases before the justices.

The Connecticut law was challenged by two gun rights groups and several individuals, who argue that both Heller and the high court’s 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association Inc. v. Bruen necessitated a finding that AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles are protected arms that cannot be banned consistent with the Second Amendment.

(Bruen held that the states could not prevent law-abiding citizens with self-defense needs from carrying firearms in public, and it reiterated Heller’s history and tradition test.)

# Supreme Court to tackle AR-15 bans in blockbuster Second Amendment case
Fourteen years after a lone gunman carried out the [deadliest elementary school shooting](https://www.cnn.com/us/connecticut-shootings-fast-facts) in American history, the Supreme Court is turning to a bitter legal fight over whether communities may outlaw the type of weapon used in that massacre — a popular class of semi-automatic guns that includes the AR-15.
In one of the most notable Second Amendment cases to reach the 6-3 conservative court in decades, the justices will hear arguments Wednesday over state and local bans on “assault-style” weapons, such as the AR-15, some of which were enacted or strengthened in response to a [dramatic increase in mass shootings](https://www.cnn.com/us/mass-shootings-fast-facts) since 20 first graders and six educators were killed in 2012 at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut.

Connecticut and Cook County are leaning into the Supreme Court’s reasoning in a 2022 precedent, [New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen](https://www.oyez.org/cases/2021/20-843), which struck down a strict requirement in New York that residents show cause to obtain a carry permit. As part of that decision, a 6-3 majority concluded that in order to survive a Second Amendment challenge, modern-day gun regulations needed to have some grounding in the “nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative who is closer to the center than Alito or Thomas, wrote in the Maryland case that the state was “something of an outlier” by having a ban on the weapons. And, he said, given that millions of Americans own one, the challengers had a “strong argument” that AR-15s are protected by the Second Amendment. As an appeals court judge in 2011, Kavanaugh also dissented from a decision upholding a Washington, DC, ban on “assault-style” rifles.

In these consolidated cases, the Court will consider “ [w]hether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles.” Cook County and Connecticut enacted laws that ban the possession of assault weapons, including AR-15s. Petitioners are individuals who would like to own weapons among those banned. In Viramontes, the district court granted summary judgment for Cook County, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed. 2025 WL 1553896. 

Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022), the Second Circuit first assumed that the assault weapons at issue fell within the meaning of the Second Amendment. 

Petitioners in both cases argue that the lower courts incorrectly applied Heller and Bruen. Petitioners contend that AR-15s are among the most commonly owned firearms in the United States and therefore cannot be classified as “dangerous and unusual weapons” excluded from the Second Amendment’s protection. Petitioners also assert that the lower courts have improperly treated Heller ’s “common use” principle as part of Bruen ’s textual inquiry. Instead, petitioners argue, the “common use” standard was “derived from the history of restricting dangerous and unusual weapons,” making it part of Bruen ’s historical-tradition analysis. Petitioners further maintain that the lower courts’ reasoning would permit legislatures to ban virtually any firearm, leaving little meaningful protection under the Second Amendment.

Respondents in both cases argue that the assault weapons bans are consistent with the Second Amendment, as the nation has a historical tradition of regulating exceptionally dangerous weapons. According to respondents, AR-15s possess characteristics that make them particularly dangerous, considering their militaristic features, popularity in mass shootings, and unsuitability for self-defense.
